claims.text: TypeSafe AI opened early access to Jev, their SystemOne model, in the week before this post (September 2026).
Jev is TypeSafe AI's SystemOne model.
TypeSafe's Jev comes with a set of AI primitives that let apps, agents, and workflows make decisions based on context.
Jev's decision-making primitives are confidence scoring, multiple choice, and yes/no (noul) questions.
GeoDeploy pairs TypeSafe Jev's confidence-gated decisions with the Pulumi Automation API to pick the best region and provision Kubernetes across AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud.
GeoDeploy is open source and available today at github.com/pulumi/devx-geodeploy.
GeoDeploy compares every AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud region that offers managed Kubernetes.

A GeoDeploy deployment request consists of target geos (traffic share and data-residency rule: EU-only, US-only, or in-country), an image with platforms (amd64, arm64, or both), a workload shape (replicas, CPU and memory per pod, egress, storage), and constraints (allowed providers, provider count, budget).
In GeoDeploy, the TypeScript app never makes judgment calls; Jev never does arithmetic, generates code, or invents region names; Pulumi never decides anything.
GeoDeploy uses great-circle distance as a coverage measure when enumerating candidate regions.
GeoDeploy fetches current prices from the AWS Price List API, the Azure Retail Prices API, and the Google Cloud Billing Catalog, normalized into a single quote format.
GeoDeploy's deterministic TypeScript bin-packs pods onto nodes, filters out instance types that don't match the image's architecture, and computes a monthly cost per candidate.
GeoDeploy assembles a Pulumi program from a curated registry of typed modules: EKS, AKS, or GKE; ECR, ACR, or Artifact Registry; ingress; DNS through Route 53, NS1, or Cloudflare; and observability.
GeoDeploy's Pulumi Automation API step runs a preview and then an update, with one stack per region.
GeoDeploy will not run provisioning unless cloud credentials pass readiness checks.
Every GeoDeploy run writes a plan.json and plan.md with the full decision record, and a web UI shows the deployment on a live globe.
Jev returns typed answers with calibrated confidence rather than free text.
Jev's choice() primitive picks one option from a closed list and returns the pick, a probability distribution across all options, and a confidence.
Jev's score() primitive rates something against a rubric you describe; GeoDeploy uses 10 levels.
Jev's noul() primitive answers a yes/no question with a single probability.
Jev only selects from closed sets and never writes code or does arithmetic, so a hallucinated region or made-up Pulumi argument can't happen by construction.
For each geo, GeoDeploy sends Jev a shortlist of up to 40 priced candidates along with constraints and the image's architecture, in a single call.

GeoDeploy's Jev call asks for one selection (choice), five quality scores (coverage, cost fit, maturity, sprawl risk, architecture consistency), two hard checks (noul: data residency and capacity), and a fallback region (choice).
GeoDeploy's question code lives in packages/decide/src/questions.ts and imports choice, noul, score from the "@typesafe-ai/sdk" package.
TypeSafe advises to "describe situations, not degrees" when writing rubrics.

GeoDeploy's rubrics use 10 levels, running from "Serves users on a different continent with no nearby presence" to "In-geo with multiple availability zones, directly in or adjacent to the demand geo's primary population center."

The TypeSafe SDK provides a TypeSafeClient with a systemOne method taking state and questions, returning answers with fields such as selection.choice, selection.confidence, residencyOk.noul, coverage.score.
GeoDeploy's ranking runs on weight profiles: latency-optimized (default), balanced, residency-first, and failure-domain.
Because GeoDeploy's weights live in code, the ranking can be re-tuned without calling Jev again.

GeoDeploy weight profiles: latency-optimized cost 0.13, coverage 0.48, maturity 0.17, sprawl 0.1, archConsistency 0.12; balanced 0.25/0.25/0.2/0.12/0.18; residency-first 0.12/0.12/0.38/0.23/0.15; failure-domain 0.08/0.17/0.48/0.15/0.12.
Every extra cloud provider means more credentials, tooling, and on-call runbooks.
In GeoDeploy, cluster and registry modules follow directly from the provider (AWS always means EKS and ECR), leaving Jev to decide ingress posture, autoscaling posture, and node-pool sizing tier.

GeoDeploy confidence thresholds: data residency 0.95 (hard reject); region for a new cluster 0.90 (top three candidates flagged for human); region when stack exists 0.75 (keep existing region); ingress or autoscaling module 0.85 (registry default); node-pool sizing tier 0.60 (bin-packing result); global floor for region pick, residency, or capacity 0.50 (drop AI path for that geo).
The residency check is in packages/decide/src/engine.ts and hard-rejects when residencyOk confidence is below 0.95.
Each AiPathAborted in GeoDeploy carries the full attempt (state, questions, and answers), so a rejected answer ends up in the audit trail.

If a gate check fails, the API times out or errors, or the upstream can't be reached, GeoDeploy switches to a deterministic fallback that compares prices across providers while still enforcing residency and constraint checks.
The `geodeploy explain` command shows why each region won.
GeoDeploy's self-driving mode is enabled via `geodeploy monitor`, and periodically checks each deployment's CPU utilization.

In self-driving mode, GeoDeploy asks Jev one joint question across all regions with options no-change, scale-up:<geo>, scale-down:<geo>, or shift:<from>-><to>, plus a separate disruption-risk check; code computes the actual node-count changes.

In self-driving mode, above 0.85 confidence the resize is applied automatically; between 0.70 and 0.85 it is suggested for human approval; below 0.70 GeoDeploy ignores Jev's pick and uses a deterministic per-region rule based on observed utilization.
CPU utilization alone is a poor autoscaling metric and is usually paired with other signals such as median end-to-end request latency and error rates once a traffic baseline is established.
See the Pulumi Automation API page at /automation/.
Pulumi Automation API docs exist at /docs/iac/automation-api/.
